rationale: Forged flight authorisations can enable unauthorised operations across the airspace, creating catastrophic collision or restricted-airspace incursion risks.
GNSS spoofing or jamming can compromise navigation across multiple aircraft and cause catastrophic airspace incursions or loss-of-control accidents.
Repeatable SQL injection can expose and corrupt mass flight-plan records, undermining operational integrity and potentially contributing to unsafe traffic management.
Manipulated weather and traffic feeds can induce unsafe routing and undetected aircraft conflicts with potentially catastrophic collision consequences.
Identity fraud can enable illegal flight authorisations and weaken operator accountability, although its direct safety impact depends on subsequent flight activity.
C2 disruption or manipulation can cause loss of control and crashes during BVLOS operations, while affecting multiple aircraft and communications links.
Audit-trail destruction impairs incident investigation and accountability, indirectly increasing safety risk by preventing effective detection and remediation.
Regulatory audit manipulation can conceal systemic violations and weaken oversight, with safety consequences emerging indirectly through continued noncompliance.
Malicious flight-controller firmware can compromise aircraft control and propagate through production or update channels, potentially causing catastrophic accidents.
Fabricated telemetry can conceal real aircraft positions and conflicts from monitoring services, undermining separation and potentially causing catastrophic collisions.
Compromised trusted suppliers can distribute persistent malicious firmware across an entire fleet, enabling widespread control compromise and catastrophic safety failures.
Poisoning the single source of truth can simultaneously corrupt dependent services, producing widespread unsafe decisions and potentially catastrophic airspace conflicts.
Sabotage of critical vertiport controls can disable landing operations and endanger aircraft and personnel, with severity depending on facility redundancy and occupancy.
Manipulated altitude or inertial measurements can corrupt flight-control decisions and cause loss of separation or aircraft crashes.
Ground-station power loss can halt operations, while malicious BMS manipulation can deplete airborne batteries and cause uncontrolled descent or crashes.
Stolen API credentials and unrestricted queries facilitate repeatable bulk disclosure of sensitive flight plans, with safety consequences primarily arising from subsequent misuse.
Removing or altering no-fly-zone records can mislead multiple operators into restricted airspace, potentially causing severe conflicts with crewed aircraft or sensitive facilities.
Strategic-document exfiltration exposes deployment plans and risk assessments that can aid adversaries, but the described disclosure has no direct safety consequence.
Flooding a single point of failure can make flight authorisations unavailable across an entire volume, disrupting safe operations and potentially stranding airborne aircraft.
Forged geofence boundaries can systematically mislead operators into restricted airspace, creating potentially catastrophic conflicts with crewed aircraft or other protected operations.

Exploiting regulatory ambiguity can enable providers to operate without adequate cybersecurity controls, increasing systemic exposure while producing indirect and context-dependent safety consequences.
